strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and underexplored problem — text-driven amodal 3D generation — that cleanly separates 'what must be preserved' (observation) from 'what is missing' (semantic completion), addressing a real limitation of feedforward image-to-3D models that collapse ambiguous occlusions to a single overfitted mode.

The dual-branch, training-free design (rigid observation branch + relaxed semantic-prior branch with visibility-aware fusion) is practical and plug-and-play, demonstrated on two different backbones (TRELLIS and SAM3D) without retraining.

Provides a theoretical narrative (low-pass relaxation via attention-logit smoothing, spectral error-reduction proposition, and Wasserstein stability bounds) that, while based on strong assumptions, gives a coherent conceptual justification for the design choices and connects nicely to the empirical corridor-smoothing intuition (Fig. 2).

Contributes two new diagnostic benchmarks (ExtremeOcc-3D and AmbiSem-3D) targeting extreme occlusion and semantic branching respectively, which could be useful community resources for evaluating controllable amodal 3D generation.

Extensive empirical validation: quantitative comparisons (CLIP scores, LPIPS, FID, Point-FID) against multiple baseline families (non-occlusion-aware, 2D-completion pipelines, occlusion-aware models), a user study (n=32) on AmbiSem-3D, thorough ablations (low-pass relaxation, visibility mask, cutoff schedule, number of priors, prior source), and many qualitative examples including an honest failure-case analysis under conflicting observation/prior evidence.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis rests on strong, largely unverified assumptions (Assumption A.2 that the oracle semantic field is band-limited, Assumption A.3 that estimation error is dominated by high frequencies, Assumption A.11 relating logit smoothing to a Lipschitz velocity change) that are asserted rather than empirically validated on the actual networks used; the formal 'proofs' mostly restate these assumptions in different notation rather than demonstrating they hold in practice, so the theoretical guarantees provide limited practical assurance beyond intuition.

Benchmark scale is small: ExtremeOcc-3D has 264 test cases and AmbiSem-3D only 21 hand-curated cases with a 32-person user study, limiting statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially for AmbiSem-3D where there is no ground truth and evaluation relies mainly on CLIP similarity and subjective user judgment.

Comparisons on AmbiSem-3D omit some occlusion-aware baselines evaluated on ExtremeOcc-3D (e.g., Amodal3R, DeOcc-1-to-3), and the multi-view TRELLIS baseline is given extra information (an additional image) not available to other methods, raising fairness concerns in the comparison setup.

The method depends on generating or retrieving multiple prior images and on backbone-provided pose estimates for the visibility mask (unavailable for TRELLIS, requiring the mask to be disabled there), introducing extra computational cost, additional external-model dependency (Z-Image for prior generation), and reduced applicability when pose/visibility information is unreliable.

Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (σ, cutoff ρ, number of priors N) is conducted only on ExtremeOcc-3D with the SAM3D backbone, leaving open how robust the default settings are across the other backbone/benchmark combinations.

The failure-mode discussion, while honest, is limited to a few illustrative morphing examples rather than a systematic quantitative characterization of how often and how severely the method fails when observation and prior conflict.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a genuine and under-studied problem: resolving semantic ambiguity in image-to-3D generation under heavy occlusion via text prompts, distinguishing it clearly from generic conditional 3D generation.

The proposed dual-branch, training-free design (observation branch + relaxed semantic-prior branch with visibility-aware fusion) is a practical plug-and-play mechanism that can be applied on top of existing feedforward backbones (TRELLIS, SAM3D) without retraining, which is appealing for deployment.

The paper contributes two new diagnostic benchmarks (ExtremeOcc-3D and AmbiSem-3D) targeting extreme occlusion and semantic branching respectively, which could be useful resources if released, since existing benchmarks do not test text-driven disambiguation.

Qualitative results (Figs. 4, 7-10) convincingly show that baselines (TRELLIS, SAM3D, 2D-edit pipelines) tend to either ignore the prompt or overfit to a single hallucinated interpretation, while the proposed method visibly follows the intended category/attribute while preserving observed geometry.

The authors include an honest failure-case analysis (Fig. 11, Appendix G) showing the method's 'soft concept fusion' behavior when observation and prior are mutually incompatible, rather than hiding this limitation.
Ablations (Table 5a, Fig. 6) probe the contribution of the low-pass relaxation, visibility mask, cutoff, and number of priors, giving some insight into design choices.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is overstated relative to what is actually proven. Assumption A.2 (semantic intent is band-limited/low-frequency) and Assumption A.3 (errors are high-frequency) are asserted without empirical or principled justification — the entire 'proof' of error reduction (Prop. A.4) and the subsequent Wasserstein bounds (Thm. A.8, A.9) follow almost tautologically once these unverified spectral assumptions are granted, so the 'low-pass filter is provably beneficial' claim is much weaker than the formal presentation suggests. The bound in Thm. A.9 also contains an uncontrolled residual term δ_prior that is never actually bounded, undermining the practical value of the guarantee.

Both introduced benchmarks are very small: AmbiSem-3D has only 21 hand-curated cases (evaluated by 32 user-study volunteers), and ExtremeOcc-3D uses 264 test cases. Reporting FID and Point-FID — distributional metrics that typically require large sample sizes to be statistically reliable — on sets of this size raises serious concerns about the robustness/significance of the reported numbers, and no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are given anywhere in the paper.

The user study (n=32, 21 cases) lacks methodological detail: no description of blinding, randomization of method order, or statistical significance testing, making the reported large preference margins (e.g., 68.52% overall) difficult to trust as rigorous evidence.

Baseline coverage is inconsistent across the two evaluation settings — e.g., Amodal3R and DeOcc-1-to-3 are compared only on ExtremeOcc-3D but not on AmbiSem-3D, and some comparisons (2D-edit-then-3D) use different underlying reconstruction backbones, complicating fair, controlled comparison.

The core technical contribution reduces to a fairly simple engineering trick (Gaussian smoothing of prior-branch cross-attention logits plus a depth-based visibility mask for blending), and the extensive formal machinery (Wasserstein-2 bounds, Grönwall's inequality, Lipschitz stability) appears disproportionate to, and only loosely connected with, this practical mechanism, giving an impression of theoretical over-dressing rather than a load-bearing theoretical contribution.

Both benchmarks are built from largely furniture/indoor-object-centric datasets (3D-FUTURE/3D-FRONT, ObjaverseXL curated subset), so generalization of the method and its evaluation to more diverse, non-furniture domains is not demonstrated.

No mention of code, benchmark, or model release, which combined with the reliance on internal implementation details (retrieval pools, prompt engineering suffixes for prior generation, several hyperparameters β, γ, λ, σ, ρ) raises reproducibility concerns.

The method's dependence on retrieved or generated 'prior images' introduces an additional failure surface (retrieval/generation quality) that is only superficially ablated (Table 5a 'Prior from generation'), without deeper analysis of robustness when priors are noisy, unavailable, or inconsistent.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formalized new problem setting (text-driven amodal 3D generation) that addresses a real limitation of existing feedforward image-to-3D models: their inability to resolve occlusion-induced semantic ambiguity via user intent.

The dual-branch decomposition (rigid observation branch vs. relaxed semantic-prior branch) is an intuitive and practical design, and the paper provides a concrete, training-free mechanism (attention-logit Gaussian smoothing) to realize it without retraining the backbone generators, making it broadly applicable as a plug-and-play module (demonstrated on both TRELLIS and SAM3D).

Reasonably thorough theoretical development connecting the relaxation mechanism to a low-pass filtering interpretation of the semantic vector field, with derivations of error-reduction propositions, Lipschitz stability, and Wasserstein-2 distance bounds, giving some principled grounding beyond a purely heuristic design.

Introduction of two new diagnostic benchmarks (ExtremeOcc-3D for extreme occlusion completion, AmbiSem-3D for semantic branching) fills a gap in existing 3D generation evaluation and could be a useful community resource for future controllable/amodal 3D generation research.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: quantitative comparisons across multiple metrics (CLIP similarity, LPIPS, FID, Point-FID) on two backbones, a user study on AmbiSem-3D, extensive ablations (low-pass relaxation, visibility mask, cutoff/sigma sensitivity, number of priors, prior source), and multiple qualitative figures across diverse object categories.
Includes an honest discussion of failure modes (conflicting observation/prior evidence) with illustrative examples, rather than only showcasing favorable cases.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis rests on strong, largely unverified assumptions (A.2 band-limited semantic signal, A.3 high-frequency-dominated error) that are asserted rather than empirically validated (e.g., no spectral/frequency-domain measurements of actual learned vs. oracle velocity fields are shown), so the formal bounds function more as motivating intuition than as a rigorous guarantee tied to the actual model's behavior.

AmbiSem-3D is very small (21 curated cases) and the user study has only 32 participants; while useful as a diagnostic proof-of-concept, this scale limits the statistical robustness of the semantic-branching claims and generalizability of the reported preference margins.

ExtremeOcc-3D construction relies on retrieving a single differing instance of the same category as the 'prior image' and on a fixed 80% occlusion threshold heuristic for filtering, which may not fully capture the diversity of real-world occlusion scenarios or guarantee that 80% is a universally meaningful ambiguity threshold across object types.

The method assumes accurate camera pose from the backbone to construct the visibility mask (Appendix E); for backbones without pose estimation (e.g., TRELLIS) the mask is simply disabled, which could limit the applicability of the full visibility-aware fusion mechanism to certain generator families.

Hyperparameters (σ, ρ, N) appear tuned per backbone/benchmark, and while ablations show some robustness, there is limited guidance or theory on how to set these for new domains, object types, or occlusion levels, raising reproducibility/generalization concerns in practice.

Failure-case analysis (Appendix G, Fig. 11) is illustrative rather than quantitative — no failure rate or systematic characterization of when the dual-branch fusion breaks down under conflicting observation/prior evidence is provided.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formalized new problem setting (text-driven amodal 3D generation) that fills a genuine gap: existing feedforward image-to-3D models collapse ambiguous occluded regions to a single overfitted mode, and this paper explicitly targets controllable disambiguation via text.
Training-free, plug-and-play design applicable to multiple existing backbones (TRELLIS, SAM3D) without retraining, which is practically appealing and lowers adoption cost.

The dual-branch decomposition (rigid observation branch vs. relaxed semantic branch), multi-prior consensus, and visibility-aware fusion are sensible engineering choices, each individually ablated (Table 6a/Fig. 5-6) to show contribution to performance.

Introduces two new diagnostic benchmarks (ExtremeOcc-3D and AmbiSem-3D) targeting extreme occlusion and semantic branching respectively, which could be useful community resources given the scarcity of such controlled evaluation settings.

Reasonably extensive empirical validation: comparisons against occlusion-aware and non-occlusion-aware baselines, several alternative baseline families (video generation, multi-view generation, commercial 2D editing + 3D, direct text+image conditioning), a 32-person user study, an extended 100-case ambiguity benchmark, and runtime/memory overhead reporting.

Includes an honest failure-mode analysis (Appendix H, Fig. 16) showing the method degrades gracefully (soft concept fusion) rather than catastrophically when observation and prior conflict, and clearly states the compatibility assumption underlying the method.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis, while extensive in the appendix, rests on strong and largely unverified assumptions (band-limited oracle semantic field, high-frequency-dominated error, global Lipschitz constants for the neural velocity estimator). The core proposition (A.4) is close to definitionally true given the assumptions (error is stipulated to be dominated by high frequency, so filtering it out trivially reduces error), so the 'proof' offers limited independent evidence beyond motivating the design choice; the practical value of the theory is mainly illustrative/intuitive rather than rigorously predictive.

Benchmark sizes are small, especially AmbiSem-3D (21 curated cases, extended to 100), limiting the statistical robustness of the reported metrics and user-study preference numbers; details of the user study protocol (blinding, randomization, inter-rater agreement) are not reported.

AmbiSem-3D has no ground-truth 3D shapes, so evaluation relies on CLIP-based automatic metrics and subjective user preference, both of which can be biased toward methods that produce plausible-looking but not necessarily geometrically correct objects.

For ExtremeOcc-3D, prior images are retrieved from the same source dataset (3D-FUTURE) used to build the test set, which could leak distributional information into the 'prior' condition and inflate the reported gains versus a purely observation-driven baseline; the robustness check with generated priors (Z-Image) only partially mitigates this concern and shows a non-trivial performance gap (Point-FID 82.7 vs 81.1).

Table 1's main comparison mixes different backbones (TRELLIS vs. SAM3D) across rows in a way that makes head-to-head comparison of 'occlusion-aware' vs 'non-occlusion-aware' categories somewhat confusing rather than a clean ablation isolating the RelaxFlow contribution alone.

The method introduces several hyperparameters (σ, ρ, N, visibility-mask parameters β, γ, λ) with defaults tuned on the reported benchmarks; while some sensitivity analysis is given, generalization to substantially different domains/object categories is not demonstrated.

The core contribution is primarily an inference-time engineering pipeline (attention-logit blurring, prior consensus, visibility-aware blending) layered on top of existing pretrained generators rather than a new generative model, which somewhat limits the conceptual novelty despite being a reasonable systems-level contribution.

Retraining-based occlusion-completion baselines (e.g., Amodal3R, DeOcc-1-to-3) are only compared on ExtremeOcc-3D, not on AmbiSem-3D, leaving open how well such methods might handle (or fail at) explicit semantic branching.

strengths: Clearly formalizes a new and practically relevant task, text-driven amodal 3D generation, distinguishing observation fidelity from prompt-following under occlusion-induced ambiguity, and motivates it with an intuitive teaser example (Fig. 1).

Proposes a training-free, plug-in dual-branch framework (RelaxFlow) that can be attached to existing feedforward image-to-3D backbones (TRELLIS, SAM3D) without retraining, which is practically attractive given the cost of retraining large 3D generators.

Extensive empirical comparisons against a wide range of baseline families: occlusion-aware/non-occlusion-aware feedforward models, 2D-edit-then-3D pipelines, video-generation-to-3D, multi-view-generation-to-3D, and a commercial 2D editor (Nano Banana Pro), plus informative qualitative failure illustrations for each (Figs. 9-12).
Reasonably thorough ablation study (component removal, hyperparameter sensitivity, number of priors, prior source) isolating the contribution of low-pass relaxation and the visibility-aware mask.
Honest discussion of failure modes (Appendix H) when observation and prior genuinely conflict, rather than hiding limitations.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis, while presented with proofs and theorems, rests on strong idealized assumptions (band-limited semantic signal A.2, high-frequency-dominant error A.3, logit-to-velocity Lipschitz smoothness A.11) that are asserted rather than empirically verified for the actual transformer backbones used; the subsequent 'proofs' are near-tautological consequences of these assumptions, so the claim 'we prove relaxation is equivalent to a low-pass filter' overstates the rigor relative to what is actually shown about the real network.

Both introduced benchmarks are very small and manually curated: AmbiSem-3D has only 21 base cases (the 100-case extension is evaluated only against SAM3D and only with CLIP metrics, not the full baseline suite or user study), and ExtremeOcc-3D has 264 filtered cases; this limits statistical confidence and raises concerns about possible cherry-picking of qualitative examples shown throughout the paper.
The user study is small (n=32) and conducted only on the 21-case AmbiSem-3D set, limiting the robustness of the human-preference claims (e.g., 68.52% overall preference).

The method introduces nontrivial additional cost and dependencies: 1.8-2.5x inference-time overhead (Table 6) and reliance on an external text-to-image generator or retrieval pool for constructing prior images, whose quality/bias could materially affect results but is not stress-tested beyond one ablation (retrieved vs. generated priors).

On the primary ExtremeOcc-3D benchmark, RelaxFlow is only 'competitive' (not better) on CLIP_img and LPIPS relative to SAM3D, indicating the claimed joint optimization of fidelity and prompt-following still involves trade-offs that are somewhat understated in the main text framing.
No mention of code or data release, which combined with the manually curated/small benchmarks raises reproducibility concerns for other researchers wishing to verify or extend the results.

The core mechanism (cross-attention logit blurring as a form of guidance smoothing) builds closely on existing smoothed-energy-guidance ideas (Hong, 2024) applied to a new dual-branch 3D setting; the technical novelty is somewhat incremental relative to the conceptual/task-formulation contribution.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated new problem formulation (text-driven amodal 3D generation) that identifies a real gap: feedforward image-to-3D models collapse to an 'observation-overfitted' mode under heavy occlusion and cannot be steered by text intent.

Training-free, plug-and-play dual-branch design (observation branch + low-pass-relaxed semantic-prior branch with visibility-aware fusion) that can be applied to multiple existing backbones (TRELLIS, SAM3D) without retraining, which is practically appealing.

A theoretical narrative connecting the proposed attention-logit blurring to a low-pass relaxation of the semantic velocity field, with derivations of error-reduction and Wasserstein-distance bounds that at least qualitatively justify the design choice.

Two new diagnostic benchmarks (ExtremeOcc-3D and AmbiSem-3D, plus a 100-case extension) target an underexplored aspect of evaluation—whether text can disambiguate occluded/ambiguous structure—which could be useful to the community beyond this paper.

Extensive empirical validation: multiple backbones, several baseline families (occlusion-aware 3D methods, 2D-completion-then-lift, video generation, multi-view generation, commercial 2D editing), ablations on every design component, a user study, efficiency/memory measurements, and an honest failure-case analysis (conflicting observation/prior) in the appendix.
Qualitative results are generally convincing and show visible improvement over the cited baselines in resolving category-level ambiguity while preserving visible structure.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis relies on fairly strong, largely unverified idealized assumptions (band-limited oracle semantic field, high-frequency-dominated error, Lipschitz logit-to-velocity mapping) and the step connecting the abstract low-pass operator to the concrete attention-logit Gaussian blur (Assumption A.11) only yields a generic Lipschitz-type bound rather than a tight guarantee; the theory is more illustrative/motivational than a rigorous proof that the specific implemented mechanism achieves the claimed benefits.

AmbiSem-3D's primary diagnostic set is very small (21 manually curated cases; extension to 100 is only lightly described and evaluated with a single metric pair in an appendix table), raising concerns about statistical robustness and potential selection bias in case curation.

Reliance on automatic 2D/3D semantic metrics (CLIP similarity, Point-FID, LPIPS) as primary quantitative evidence is a known weak proxy for actual 3D geometric/semantic correctness; human evaluation is only conducted for AmbiSem-3D (n=32) and not for the main ExtremeOcc-3D benchmark.

The method introduces several additional hyperparameters (number of priors N, cutoff ratio ρ, blur strength σ) whose sensitivity is shown to matter (Table/Figure 6), suggesting some brittleness and extra tuning burden for new domains/backbones.

Non-trivial runtime overhead (1.8x–2.5x increase, Table 6) and the need for external prior-image sources (retrieval pool or text-to-image generation) add practical deployment cost not fully contextualized against benefits.

The method's fusion mechanism is a heuristic (linear cutoff schedule, visibility-based Gaussian falloff) rather than something derived directly from the theory, so the gap between the theoretical story and the concrete engineering choices (schedule, thresholds) is not fully closed.

Comparisons with some baseline families (video generation, commercial 2D editing) may be somewhat unfair since those pipelines are not designed for this exact task, which the authors acknowledge but which still limits how much can be concluded from those specific comparisons.
